question: Three broken bones: one held rigid, one allowed to flex a little, one flexing a lot. Which grows a big bony callus?
answer: The one flexing a little. Callus, a bridging collar of new bone, forms when the gap flexes by roughly 2 to 10% of its width. Held rigid, a break knits directly with little callus; flexing much more, it fills with fibrous tissue and may never unite. Surgeons choose their fixings partly by this rule.
move: Some strain is the signal to build; none, or too much, stops it.
trap: Assuming stiller is always better, so the rigid one grows most bone.
reference: Perren, Physical and biological aspects of fracture healing with special reference to internal fixation, Clinical Orthopaedics and Related Research, 1979
